description: Single transcript. A civil exchange with reasoned positions on both sides and nothing to flag (no planted problems). Expected: no issues, no intervention.

topic.title: Rent control
topic.proposition: Cities should cap how much landlords can raise rents each year.

messages.author: Participant A
messages.text: I think rent control is worth trying because sudden increases can uproot families, and stability has a value for a community beyond what a market price shows. I know it has costs, and I would like to hear which ones you find most serious.

messages.author: Participant B
messages.text: Thank you for putting it that way. My main worry is what happens to the supply of housing over time. If owners expect limits on future rents, they may build less or convert buildings to other uses, and that hurts people looking for a home. I would still like to find some way to protect tenants from sharp increases.

messages.author: Participant A
messages.text: That is a fair worry. Perhaps we can agree that protection from sudden jumps is a shared goal, and disagree about the tool. Would you be more open to a cap that applies only to older buildings and rises with inflation?

messages.author: Participant B
messages.text: I would be more open to that, yes. Older buildings that are already standing are not affected by the incentive to build, so my main worry would be smaller. I would still want the cap reviewed regularly, so we can see how it works and adjust it if it causes problems.
